title: How Do Tax Brackets Work? A $1,000 Raise, $170 More Income Tax
description: A higher tax bracket never lowers your take-home pay. 2026 IRS brackets, a $1,000 raise into the 22% bracket, and marginal vs effective rate, explained with real math.
answer: Only the dollars above each bracket line pay the higher rate. A $1,000 raise that crosses into the 22% bracket adds just $170 of federal income tax in our 2026 example, so the person still keeps about $830 after federal income tax.
takeaways: 2026 single brackets run from 10% to 37%; the standard deduction is $16,100.
On an $80,000 salary: taxable income $63,900, federal income tax $8,770, effective rate 11.0%, marginal rate 22%.
With Social Security and Medicare (7.65%), the raise still adds about $753.50 to pay.
faq: Will a raise put me in a higher tax bracket and lower my take-home pay?

With federal income tax brackets alone, no. Only the part of your taxable income above a bracket line is taxed at the higher rate, so a raise always adds take-home pay. Separate rules, like credits that phase out as income rises, work differently.
What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?

The marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar of taxable income. The effective rate here is your total federal income tax divided by your salary. On an $80,000 salary in 2026 (single, standard deduction), they are 22% and about 11%.

title: Paying Only the Minimum on $8,000? The 23-Year Credit Card Math
description: Paying only the minimum on an $8,000 credit card can cost about $21,800 and take 23 years. The month-by-month math, with official Federal Reserve and CFPB sources.
answer: In our simulation, paying only the minimum on $8,000 at 22.36% APR takes 278 months (about 23 years) and costs about $21,831. Simply keeping the first minimum payment fixed at $229 clears it in 57 months.
takeaways: Average rate on card accounts charged interest: 22.36% (Federal Reserve G.19, Aug 2026 data).
Interest on $8,000 at that rate: about $4.90 a day, roughly $149 a month.
Minimum only: $13,831 of interest. A fixed $300 a month: 38 months, about $11,163 total.
Your statement's minimum payment warning shows how long the minimum takes on your own card.
faq: How long does it take to pay off a credit card paying only the minimum?
It depends on your balance, APR and your issuer's minimum formula. In our example ($8,000, 22.36% APR, 1% of balance plus interest with a $25 floor), it takes 278 months, about 23 years.
Why does the minimum payment take so long?
As the balance falls, the minimum falls too, so less goes to the debt each month. In our example about 65% of each minimum payment is interest.
How do I avoid credit card interest on purchases?
Most cards have a grace period: paying the full statement balance by the due date usually means no interest on purchases, according to the CFPB.
